title: The Talkies Arrive
summary: For more than 30 years, movie actors could move and make faces but could not be heard. Inventors tried giant records, then learned to turn sound into a wiggly stripe of light right on the film. In 1927 Al Jolson sang and spoke in The Jazz Singer, and within a few years almost every movie in America could talk.

sections.heading: A Dream as Old as the Movies
paragraphs: You may have read that the first movies were 'silent'. In Part 12 you learned that this is not really true: theaters filled the air with piano, organ or orchestra music, and sometimes with sound effects and live narrators. What early films could not do was carry their own sound. When an actor opened her mouth on screen, nobody in the audience could hear the actual words. For about 30 years, inventors chased the dream of fixing that.

The dream is almost as old as moving pictures themselves. Thomas Edison was already famous for inventing the phonograph in 1877, a machine that recorded sound as tiny wiggles on a cylinder. When his laboratory began working on moving pictures, the idea was to do for the eyes what the phonograph had done for the ears, and then put the two together. In about 1894 or 1895, William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, whom you met in Part 10, made a short test film at Edison's lab in New Jersey. In it, Dickson plays a violin into a huge recording horn while two men dance nearby. It is known today as the Dickson Experimental Sound Film, and it is one of the oldest films made with recorded sound meant to go with it.

Edison's company even sold a version of its peephole Kinetoscope with a phonograph inside, so a viewer could look through the eyepiece while listening through rubber ear tubes. But the sound and pictures were not truly linked, and it was not a big success. In 1913 Edison tried again with the Kinetophone, which connected a projector in the booth to a phonograph behind the screen using a long belt and pulleys. If the belt slipped, or the film had been cut and repaired, the voices drifted out of step with the lips. Operators often struggled to keep it in sync, the novelty soon wore off, and after a fire at Edison's works in December 1914 destroyed its masters, the system was dropped.

In France, Léon Gaumont showed his Chronophone, which linked a projector to a record player, in 1902, and he kept improving it for years. Other inventors in Germany, Britain and the United States tried similar ideas. All of them ran into the same two giant problems.

The first problem was synchronization, or 'sync': keeping sound and picture in perfect step. Our brains are very sensitive to this. If a voice is even a fraction of a second early or late, people notice at once. The second problem was loudness. Before the 1920s, sound was recorded and played back mechanically. A singer bellowed into a horn, the sound waves shook a needle, and on playback the needle shook a horn again. That might fill a parlor, but not a theater with a thousand seats. Nobody could make the sound big enough. Solving that would take electronics.

sections.heading: Writing Sound with Light
paragraphs: One clever idea was to put the sound right onto the film itself. Then the sound and the pictures could never drift apart, because they would be on the same strip, moving through the projector together. A French-born inventor working in England, Eugene Lauste, received a patent for recording sound on film in 1907 and made experimental recordings, but he never turned it into a working business.

The electronics that made sound film possible came partly from radio. In 1906 the American inventor Lee de Forest created the Audion, a vacuum tube that could make weak electrical signals stronger. Improved tubes like it became the heart of amplifiers, the devices that take a tiny signal from a microphone and boost it until it can drive a big loudspeaker. Electrical microphones, amplifiers and loudspeakers improved quickly in the late 1910s and early 1920s, thanks to the boom in telephones and radio broadcasting.

Think of an amplifier like a person controlling a big water tap. A tiny push from a microphone's weak signal tells the tap how far to open, and a powerful flow of electricity from the mains comes out the other side, rising and falling in exactly the same pattern as the small signal, only much stronger. That stronger signal can shake the paper cone of a loudspeaker hard enough to fill a theater with sound. Without amplifiers, no sound system could have reached the back row of a big cinema.

De Forest then turned to film. Working with an inventor named Theodore Case, who had developed sensitive light-detecting tubes, he created a sound-on-film system he called Phonofilm. Its first commercial screening took place at the Rivoli Theater in New York on 15 April 1923. Phonofilm shorts showed vaudeville performers, singers, comedians and even politicians giving speeches. People were impressed by the novelty, but the sound quality was poor, and Hollywood's big studios were not interested. De Forest and Case also quarrelled and split up. In Germany, three inventors developed a similar system called Tri-Ergon, which also struggled at first.

Phonofilm did not conquer the movies, but it proved the idea could work. The next big push came from a much larger organization: the research labs of the American telephone giant. And it came from an unexpected direction, a record.

sections.heading: Vitaphone: Giant Records and Don Juan
paragraphs: In the mid-1920s, engineers at Western Electric and its research arm, Bell Telephone Laboratories, had developed excellent electrical recording, amplifiers and loudspeakers. They built a system that recorded sound onto large discs, carefully linked to a film projector. Most Hollywood studios were not interested. But one smaller, ambitious studio was: Warner Bros., run by four brothers, Harry, Albert, Sam and Jack Warner. Sam Warner was especially excited by sound. In 1925 Warner Bros. took on the system and named it Vitaphone.

Vitaphone was a sound-on-disc system. For each reel of film, there was a matching record. The records were big, 16 inches across, about 40 centimeters, much larger than ordinary records of the time, and they spun at 33 1/3 revolutions per minute, slower than the usual 78. That combination was chosen so one disc could play for about 11 minutes, the length of one reel of film. Decades later, the same 33 1/3 speed was used for long-playing LP records, which many people still collect today.

Keeping the disc and film together took care. The turntable was mechanically connected to the projector motor, so both ran at the same speed. At the start of each reel, the projectionist lined up a marked start frame in the film with an arrow-marked start groove on the record, and then started them together. As long as nothing went wrong, the sound stayed in sync.

Recording for Vitaphone was nerve-racking. On the set, the sound was cut straight into a soft wax master disc while the camera filmed, so each scene had to be performed in one go. There was no easy way to snip out a cough or a fluffed line, as you can with a modern recording. If something went wrong, the whole take, picture and sound, was usually done again. Engineers listened in a separate room, watching dials and warning the director if the sound was too loud, too soft or spoiled by a noise from outside.

Things did go wrong, though. A disc could wear out after about 20 plays. It could crack or break. If a film broke and the projectionist cut out a few damaged frames to repair it, the picture would be slightly ahead of the record for the rest of the reel, and an actor's words would suddenly come from the wrong face. Discs also had to be shipped to every theater with every print.

Warner Bros. launched Vitaphone in New York in early August 1926 with a grand show. First came a program of short films: a filmed speech by Will Hays, the head of the film industry's trade association, welcoming the new invention, followed by famous musicians and opera singers performing. Then came the main feature, Don Juan, a swashbuckling adventure starring John Barrymore. Don Juan had no spoken dialogue. The actors still spoke through intertitles. But it had a full recorded orchestral score, played by the New York Philharmonic, and synchronized sound effects such as clashing swords and ringing bells.

Audiences were delighted, especially by the short musical films. For the first time, a small-town theater with no orchestra could offer the same music as a grand palace in New York. Even so, many people in Hollywood thought recorded music was a nice extra rather than a revolution. That changed a little over a year later.

sections.heading: You Ain't Heard Nothin' Yet
paragraphs: On the evening of 6 October 1927, crowds gathered outside Warner Bros.' theater on Broadway in New York for the premiere of The Jazz Singer. The story was about Jakie Rabinowitz, the son of a Jewish cantor, the singer who leads prayers in a synagogue. His father wants him to follow family tradition, but Jakie loves jazz and popular songs. He changes his name to Jack Robin and tries to become a star on the stage, torn between his family and his dreams.

The star was Al Jolson, then one of the most famous entertainers in America. Like Don Juan, most of the film was silent, with intertitles and a recorded music score. But in a few scenes, Jolson sang, and the audience heard his real voice coming from the screen, perfectly in time with his lips. He sang six songs, including 'Toot, Toot, Tootsie' and 'Blue Skies', and the film also included the Jewish prayer 'Kol Nidre'.

Then came the moments that made history. Before one song, Jolson spoke, apparently adding some lines of his own. 'Wait a minute, wait a minute, you ain't heard nothin' yet!' he says to the crowd in the scene. In another scene, he chats excitedly to his mother at the piano. In total, the film has only about two minutes of synchronized talking. It was not the first sound film and it was not a full 'talkie'. But hearing a star speak casually and naturally, as if he were really there, thrilled audiences in a way that recorded music alone had not.

There is an important and uncomfortable part of this story that we should be honest about. In several scenes, Jolson's character performs in blackface, wearing dark makeup to imitate and mock Black people, a custom from old minstrel shows. It was common in American entertainment at the time, and Jolson often performed this way. Today it is widely recognized as racist, because it turned Black Americans into crude stereotypes for white audiences' amusement while Black performers themselves were shut out of many opportunities. The Jazz Singer is a landmark in technology, and it is also a reminder that famous 'firsts' can carry the prejudices of their time.

The night also held a personal tragedy. Sam Warner, the brother who had pushed hardest for sound, died of pneumonia the day before the premiere, aged only 40. The other brothers were in California for his funeral and missed the triumph he had worked toward.

And it was a triumph. The Jazz Singer cost about 422,000 dollars to make and earned roughly 2.6 million dollars in rentals around the world. Every studio in Hollywood took notice. When the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences held its very first awards ceremony, a quick dinner of about 15 minutes at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel on 16 May 1929, Warner Bros. received a special honorary award for producing The Jazz Singer, which the Academy called the pioneer outstanding talking picture.

sections.heading: Sound on Film: The Wiggly Stripe
paragraphs: Vitaphone's big records had shown that people wanted sound. But the cleverer long-term answer was the one Lauste and de Forest had chased: put the sound on the film itself. Two systems in particular made it work. Fox's Movietone grew out of Theodore Case's work with his assistant Earl Sponable, after Case split from de Forest. RCA Photophone was developed from research at General Electric. Both stored sound as an optical soundtrack, a narrow strip running down the film beside the pictures.

Here is how an optical soundtrack works. Sound is made of vibrations, pressure waves in the air that rise and fall hundreds or thousands of times a second. A microphone turns those vibrations into an electrical signal that rises and falls in the same pattern. In the recording machine, that signal controls a beam of light shining onto the moving film. There were two main methods. In variable density recording, the beam got brighter and dimmer, so the soundtrack came out as a row of fine stripes, from pale gray to dark. In variable area recording, which RCA used, the beam stayed the same brightness but changed its width, so the soundtrack came out as a wavy, mountain-range shape of clear and black. If you look closely at old 35mm film, you can sometimes see that wavy line running beside the frames.

In the projector, the process runs backward. A small, steady lamp called the exciter lamp shines through the soundtrack as the film moves past. Where the track is clear, lots of light gets through. Where it is dark, less does. On the other side sits a photoelectric cell, a device that turns light into electricity: more light, more current. So the flickering light becomes a rising and falling electrical signal, exactly copying the original sound wave. Amplifiers make it stronger, and loudspeakers behind the screen turn it back into vibrations in the air. Sound becomes electricity, then light, then a pattern on film, then light, then electricity, and finally sound again.

There is one neat detail. The picture has to stop still for a split second in front of the lens for every frame, as you learned in Part 11, but sound has to be read while the film moves smoothly and steadily. So the sound reader sits a little way away from the picture gate, where the film runs smoothly, and the soundtrack is printed slightly ahead of the picture it belongs to.

Sound on film also fixed the speed of the movies. In the silent era, cameras and projectors were often cranked by hand at varying speeds. But sound has to play at exactly the speed it was recorded, or voices become squeaky or slow and growly. The coming of sound set 24 frames per second as the standard speed for sound films, and it has stayed the standard for most movies ever since.

Fox also used Movietone for feature films. Sunrise (1927), a beautiful drama directed by the German filmmaker F. W. Murnau, was released with a recorded Movietone music score and sound effects running on the film itself. Meanwhile, the other big studios had been waiting to see which system would win before spending money. In 1928, most of them agreed to adopt sound-on-film equipment from Western Electric, a decision that helped make optical soundtracks the industry standard.

Fox put Movietone to work in exciting ways. In 1927 its sound newsreels let audiences hear real events, including the roar of Charles Lindbergh's plane taking off on his famous flight across the Atlantic. Imagine sitting in a theater and hearing the engine of a plane you had only read about in newspapers. Sound on film was cheaper and more reliable than discs, and by 1931 even Warner Bros. had switched to it. The giant Vitaphone records became museum pieces, though some have since been rediscovered and matched again with their films.

sections.heading: The Great Switch
paragraphs: After The Jazz Singer, Hollywood raced to catch up. On 6 July 1928, Warner Bros. released Lights of New York, a gangster story directed by Bryan Foy. It was short, about 57 minutes, and cheap, made for about 23,000 dollars. Critics noticed the stiff acting, as performers seemed to huddle close to hidden microphones. But it had something no feature had had before: every scene had spoken dialogue. It was the first 'all-talking' feature film, and it earned more than a million dollars.

Studios now poured money into sound. They built soundproof stages, bought recording equipment and hired engineers from telephone and radio companies. Theaters had to be wired too, with new projectors, amplifiers and loudspeakers, which was expensive. In the United States, the number of theaters equipped for sound rose from about 100 to about 800 between 1928 and 1929, and by 1930 roughly half of American theaters could play sound films. Big city theaters converted first; small-town halls followed later.

Production changed even faster. By around 1930, almost every Hollywood film was being made with sound, and studios largely stopped making new silent features. In a few years, an art form that had developed for three decades without spoken words was transformed. Other countries followed at different speeds. Britain had more than 60 percent of its theaters equipped by the end of 1930, while many theaters in France and the Soviet Union stayed silent for some years longer.

Talking pictures also raised a new problem: language. A silent film could be shown anywhere by simply swapping the intertitle cards. A talkie spoke only one language. In the early sound years, some studios solved this by filming the same story several times, in English, German, Spanish and French, sometimes on the same sets at night with different actors. Later, dubbing, recording new voices in another language, and subtitles became the usual answers.

Many early sound films have had a strange afterlife. Because the Vitaphone discs were stored separately from the film reels, the two were often separated over the years. Sometimes a film survived without its records, and sometimes records survived without their film. Since 1991, a group of collectors and archivists called the Vitaphone Project has hunted for lost discs in attics, basements and collections, so that films silent for decades can be reunited with their sound and heard again.

sections.heading: Growing Pains: Booths, Microphones and Missing Musicians
paragraphs: The switch to sound was exciting, but it was also messy. The first problem was noise. Film cameras whirred and clattered, and the new sensitive microphones picked up every sound. So the cameras were locked inside soundproof booths, little rooms with a glass window, where the camera operator worked in the heat. Since the booth could not easily move, early talkies often look stiff, with long scenes filmed from one position. Soon engineers built soundproof covers called blimps that fit around the camera itself, and the camera could move again.

The second problem was microphones. Early microphones could not pick up sound from far away, and they were fixed in place. Sound engineers hid them in flower vases, lamps and other props, and actors had to stay near them, speaking toward them. Turn your head the wrong way and your line might vanish. Later, the boom microphone, a microphone on a long pole held above the actors just out of the picture, let performers move naturally again.

The third problem was voices. Silent stars had been chosen for their faces, their movements and their charm, not their voices. Now every accent, lisp or squeaky note could be heard. Some silent stars adapted easily, and stage-trained actors who knew how to speak clearly were suddenly in demand. Others found their careers fading, sometimes because their voices did not match the image audiences had imagined, and sometimes simply because studios wanted new faces. The movie Singin' in the Rain, made in 1952, is a famous comedy about exactly this moment, though it exaggerates for laughs.

The fourth problem was harder for many families. Thousands of musicians had earned their living playing in theater orchestras, or as organists and pianists accompanying silent films. When a film carried its own recorded music, theater owners no longer needed to pay them. Within a few years, many of those jobs disappeared. In Japan, the benshi, popular live narrators who explained and voiced silent films for audiences, lost their work too. New technology often brings both wonder and hardship, and the talkies brought plenty of both.

Not everyone rushed to talk. Charlie Chaplin, whose Little Tramp character was loved around the world, worried that giving the Tramp a voice would spoil him. Part of the Tramp's magic was that anyone, in any country, could understand him without words. Chaplin was so doubtful that he told a reporter he would give the talkies three years, that's all. Because he paid for and controlled his own films, he could choose for himself. His film City Lights, which premiered in January 1931, had a recorded soundtrack with music that Chaplin composed himself, plus sound effects, but no spoken dialogue. It was a huge success, and many critics today think it is his greatest film. Chaplin was a rare exception, though, and even he finally made a full talking picture, The Great Dictator, in 1940.

By the early 1930s, then, the movies had found their voices. Actors spoke, singers sang, guns banged and doors slammed. And one small studio in Los Angeles was thinking about something different. Why should only actors make sounds? What if drawings could whistle, sing and dance in perfect time with music? In that studio, a cheerful cartoon mouse was about to start whistling at the wheel of a steamboat.

deepDive: Why did sound-on-film beat sound-on-disc? Engineering, mostly. With a disc, synchronization depends on mechanics staying perfect for a whole reel: a single splice that removes damaged frames throws the lips off for everything after it, and a scratched or broken record ruins a show. An optical track is physically locked to its frames, survives splicing (losing only a blip of sound), is printed in the same lab step as the pictures, and costs almost nothing to copy. Its weaknesses were noise and range. Dust, scratches and film grain all add hiss and crackle, and the early tracks could reproduce only a limited range of frequencies, which is one reason 1930s films sound thin and boxy to modern ears. Engineers spent decades improving this: noise-reduction methods, stereo tracks squeezed into the same strip, and later digital soundtracks printed in other spaces on the film. The variable-density versus variable-area contest is a nice example of competing standards: Western Electric favored density, RCA favored area, and both companies licensed their systems widely, which kept prints playable on either type of equipment because readers simply measure the total light passing through. Historians also debate how sudden the 'coming of sound' really was. Sound experiments went back more than 30 years, Fox's Movietone newsreels and Warner's Vitaphone shorts had already familiarized audiences with recorded sound before The Jazz Singer, and the transition took several years and varied hugely by country. In Japan, silent films with benshi narrators remained common into the mid-1930s. Some film scholars argue that early talkies were a step backward artistically, because booths and fixed microphones froze camera movement that silent filmmakers had made fluid, while others point out that within about five years directors were moving cameras freely again and using sound creatively, with off-screen voices, sound effects that told part of the story, and musical numbers that could only exist in sound cinema.
funFact: The very first Academy Awards ceremony, held on 16 May 1929 at the Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel, lasted only about 15 minutes, and one of its special awards went to Warner Bros. for The Jazz Singer.
